current_roster.description: Collection of blood and urine samples for research purposes may allow us to better understand the causes of cancer in pets and may lead to improvements in the detection, diagnosis, and treatment of canine tumors. Additionally, evaluation of blood and urine can help us to determine efficacy of novel procedures such as prostate embolization.
current_roster.tagline: Help us collect blood and urine to study a new surgical technique!
current_roster.name: Looking at a new treatment and assessing the outcome through blood and urine in dogs with prostate cancer

current_roster.description: Megaesophagus literally means large or giant esophagus and refers to a syndrome in which the muscles of the esophagus lose their tone and are no longer able to propel food and water from the mouth into the stomach. This disease is common in large-breed dogs in particular and can occur at any age. While some other diseases can cause megaesophagus, in over 50% of dogs no underlying or treatable cause is identified (known as idiopathic-acquired megaesophagus). As such, no targeted therapy can be implemented. Few advancements have been made in recommendations for disease management with current suggestions documented to be inadequate. We are assessing esophageal and lower esophageal sphincter (LES) function to optimize management of megaesophagus (ME) using novel medical therapies.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find better ways of treating dogs with megaesophagus!
current_roster.name: Assessing and managing megaesophagus in dogs

current_roster.description:
When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. The objectives of this study are to 1) describe the procedure of TACE  using a novel treatment agent in a group of dogs with naturally-occurring liver cancer, and 2) evaluate the effect that liver TACE has on clinical signs, size and viability of the tumor.

Demonstrating the feasibility and efficacy of liver TACE to improve clinical signs and decrease tumor size and volume can significantly advance our treatment of this difficult disease process, as current treatment options are limited and lack efficacy. Additionally, liver TACE is minimally invasive and provides many potential advantages over traditional surgical therapies.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn more about this new technique that could shrink liver tumors in dogs!
current_roster.name: Assessing a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs

current_roster.description:
Cancer resulting in obstruction of the lower urinary tract of dogs is most commonly found in the prostate, urinary bladder and urethra (tube responsible for draining urine out of the body). Unfortunately, cancer of the lower urinary tract often results in complete blockage of the urethra, causing a patient to be unable to pass urine. The inability to urinate is a life-threatening emergency.

The placement of urethral stents is generally performed with fluoroscopic-guidance (use of “real-time” x-rays). While fluoroscopy is useful for stent placement, there may be other techniques that could be considered. Traditionally, ultrasonographic assessment of tumor size and location has been performed by transabdominal ultrasound (where the ultrasound probe is placed on the abdominal wall to allow for visualization of organs within the abdomen), but this method can be inaccurate. The use of transrectal ultrasound (where an ultrasound probe is placed into the rectum) circumvents these previously discussed problems, and therefore, the purpose of this study is to evaluate this technique for efficacy.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study a new technique to place urethral stents in dogs with prostate, bladder, and/or urethra tumors!
current_roster.name: Surgical technique to place urethral stents in dogs with prostate, bladder and/or urethra tumors

current_roster.description:
Please note that we have many inquiries coming through for this study, with limited spaces left. We ask that you be patient as we sort through inquires and do our best to get back to each individual.

Please note we are only enrolling cats diagnosed with the DRY form of FIP at this time

Pets and their owners must reside within close proximity of Davis, CA. Before we can enroll your cat, we require a full set of veterinary records to be sent to our office by your veterinarian.

Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is a fatal disease of cats with no available FDA-approved treatment or vaccine. Antiviral drugs that decrease virus replication have been investigated in cats with FIP with promising results. In this trial, your cat will receive an investigational oral antiviral drug.

If you are looking for more information on current FIP treatments and news, please visit this site: https://ccah.vetmed.ucdavis.edu/cats/resources/general-feline-infectious-peritonitis-resources.
current_roster.tagline: FIP
current_roster.name: Help us assess an antiviral drug for treating FIP in cats.

current_roster.description: The CAALM Study is evaluating the safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy of a novel dog PDL1 antibody (UCD-PDL1). This cutting-edge trial seeks to optimize dosing while exploring the antibody’s potential to improve survival outcomes for dogs with oral melanoma that has spread to the lungs.
current_roster.tagline: Pioneering hope for dogs with metastatic cancer
current_roster.name: Innovative Immunotherapy for Canine Lung Metastases: The CAALM Study

current_roster.description:
Cats with chronic itching are often difficult to treat because there are very few safe and effective anti-itch medications available for feline patients. This study aims to better understand the biology behind moderate to severe itch in cats and support the development of new treatment options.


Researchers at the UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine are partnering with the Scripps Research Institute to study molecules in the blood that may contribute to itching. By comparing samples from itchy cats and healthy cats, this research may help identify new targets for medications that can bring relief and improve quality of life for cats in the future.
current_roster.tagline: Advancing care and comfort for cats with allergic skin disease.
current_roster.name: Developing Better Treatments for Cats with Itchy Skin

current_roster.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.
current_roster.tagline: A research study evaluating a novel drug alongside radiation therapy for dogs with brain tumors.
current_roster.name: CARE Trial: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation therapy to improve Efficacy in Canine Glioma
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to compare the treatment of ear sarcoids in horses to see if the addition of photodynamic therapy (PDT) provides a lower rate of recurrence and faster healing time compared to regular laser excision. Sarcoids are the most common type of cancer identified in horses.


Tumors may be quiescent for a period of time, but most eventually become aggressive and highly invasive, extending into surrounding tissues and causing significant discomfort. Several treatment methods have been used to treat sarcoids, including surgical removal, cryotherapy, laser therapy, topical and local injectable chemotherapies, electrochemotherapy, and immunotherapy. When managing sarcoids on the ear, recurrence remains a concern, as wide tissue margins are necessary to ensure optimal outcomes. Obtaining large surgical margins in the inner and outer ears can be challenging due to the ear's contour. 


Combining photodynamic therapy (PDT) with diode laser excision may offer enhanced disease control. PDT uses light of a specific wavelength to target a dye that has been applied to the cancerous tissues and kills the cancer cells after activation with the laser. It is anticipated that the addition of PDT to diode laser tumor removal will provide better disease control (lower recurrence) and improve surgical wound healing. Sarcoid treatment that offers improved disease control and faster wound healing would be beneficial in areas that are often difficult to treat, such as the ear. If the use of PDT improves outcomes in this subset of horses, the treatment could be applied to select sarcoids in other anatomic locations.
current_roster.tagline: Ear sarcoid treatment in horses
current_roster.name: Comparing laser removal with and without photodynamic therapy for the treatment of ear sarcoids in horses
current_roster.top_investigator: Lauren Charnock, Assistant Professor of Veterinary Ophthalmology

current_roster.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.
current_roster.tagline: New treatment with autologous FAP CAR T-cells for sarcomas
current_roster.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
current_roster.top_investigator: Rachel Brady, DVM, PhD, Assistant Professor

current_roster.description: Bilateral corneal stromal loss (BCSL) is a potentially progressive ocular disease that can be associated with pain, vision loss and even loss of the eye. The objective of this study is to determine the role genetics plays in BCSL in Friesian horses. This study is designed to determine the incidence of BCSL in the breed, to determine the mode of inheritance if a single gene is involved, and identify candidate genes for further investigation.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find out why Friesians are at a higher risk of getting bilateral corneal stromal loss!
current_roster.name: Understanding the genetics causing bilateral corneal stromal loss in Friesian horses

current_roster.description: Sudden acquired retinal degeneration syndrome (SARDS) is a common cause of permanent blindness in dogs. Dogs usually present with rapid onset of blindness with no obvious abnormalities in the retina; however, the underlying cause for SARDS is unknown and no treatment exists. We are interested in characterizing this disease better with hopes of identifying protein biomarkers and/or the genetic components of this disease.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand SARDS better!
current_roster.name: Understanding Sudden Acquired Retinal Degeneration Syndrome in dogs

current_roster.description:
Tears from the ocular surface are drained from the eye through several important structures collectively known as the nasolacrimal apparatus (NLA). This frequently becomes blocked and sometimes infected leading to discomfort, tear staining, eye discharge, and skin inflammation, all of which are associated with a decreased quality of life. Clinically, NLA obstructions can be very frustrating to treat and can often lead to permanent obstruction.

We have established a team at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital consisting of specialists with expertise in Ophthalmology, Internal Medicine, Endoscopy, Diagnostic Imaging, and Interventional Radiology and have utilized fluoroscopy to successfully treat NLA obstruction in dogs. We have utilized fluoroscopy, CT, and endoscopy and capitalized on improvements in instrumentation and minimally invasive techniques developed for catheterization of other challenging locations such as the ureters to successfully treat NLA obstruction.

Based upon the success of this initial pilot study, we have initiated a clinical trial to recruit and treat more cases and to evaluate more objective outcome measures.
current_roster.tagline: Help us assess a new treatment that's less invasive for NLA blockages!
current_roster.name: A multi-disciplinary, minimally-invasive treatment for nasolacrimal apparatus (NLA) blockage

current_roster.description: When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial embolization (TAE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to 1) describe the procedure of TAE in a group of dogs with naturally-occurring liver cancer, and 2) evaluate the effect that liver TAE has on clinical signs, size and viability of the tumor.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn more about this new technique that could shrink liver tumors in dogs!
current_roster.name: Using a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether three times weekly dosing with oral rapamycin can reverse the heart muscle changes associated with subvalvular aortic stenosis (SAS) in dogs.  As the current treatment options are limited in this disease, this has the potential to provide further treatment options to improve quantity and quality of life in this disease.
current_roster.name: Assessing an Oral Drug to Reverse Subvalvular Aortic Stenosis (SAS) in Dogs

current_roster.description:
The corneal endothelium is a thin layer of cells at the posterior aspect of the 
cornea responsible for keeping the cornea dehydrated and thus transparent, 
providing clear vision. Corneal endothelial disease can lead to corneal swelling 
(edema), painful corneal blisters (bullous keratopathy) and increased risk of 
postoperative complications after cataract surgeries that may lead to loss of 
vision. Despite advances in cataract surgical techniques, corneal endothelial cell 
damage can occur during the surgery, exacerbating pre-existing endothelial 
disease. Thus, patients with preexisting endothelial disease are at increased risk 
of postoperative complications and it is extremely important to detect low 
corneal endothelial cell density and endothelial disease early.
Early detection of corneal endothelial disease is possible by screening with in 
vivo confocal microscopy (an emerging noninvasive imaging and diagnostic tool) 
and may allow clinicians and owners to make personalized decisions regarding 
close monitoring or institution of therapies to delay disease progression.
current_roster.tagline: Early detection of corneal endothelial disease in dogs
current_roster.name: Help researchers detect early corneal endothelial disease through advanced imaging techniques
current_roster.top_investigator: Bianca Da Costa Martins, DVM, PhD, DACVO

current_roster.description:
Nasal tumors can cause severe nasal bleeding or discharge and difficulty breathing. These tumors often aggressively spread throughout the tissues of the nasal cavity and into the surrounding organs, including the eye and brain. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for nasal tumors in dogs; however, radiation therapy isn't often good for long-term control of the tumor. An another treatment option is transarterial embolization, or TAE, which involves the delivery of a mechanical “clot” to the main arteries supplying blood to the tissues of the nasal cavity with the goal of eliminating the blood supply of the tumor and decreasing tumor size.

The purposes of this study are to 1) describe TAE in dogs with naturally-occurring nasal cancer, 2) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the tumor, and 3) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the values measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.
current_roster.tagline: Help us treat nasal tumors in dogs using a new kind of therapy!
current_roster.name: Novel Treatment for Nasal Tumors

current_roster.description: This VMTH clinical trial is investigating the effect of nicotinamide (vitamin B3) given by mouth alone or in combination with a topical drop, ripasudil, that we have previously shown to be effective for the treatment of corneal endothelial disease (CED) in dogs. Dogs with CED have corneal swelling which can decrease their vision. They also can develop corneal ulcers which causes pain and these can become infected. Corneal transplant surgery is the most effective treatment for this disease, but there is limited available donor tissue, and the graft can be rejected. Another surgical option, superficial keratectomy and advancement hood flap (SKAHF), is palliative and does not address the underlying problem. Thus, we need to investigate new medical treatments for CED. We hope that oral nicotinamide alone, or in combination with topical ripasudil, will delay or reverse CED progression.
current_roster.name: Investigating new therapies for dogs with corneal endothelial disease

current_roster.description:
Canine Cutaneous Epitheliotropic T-cell Lymphoma (CETCL) is a rare but aggressive skin cancer in dogs, and sadly, most affected dogs live less than a year after diagnosis, even with chemotherapy. One major reason for this poor prognosis is that we don’t fully understand how the disease develops or progresses, which has made it difficult to create new, effective treatments.

This study aims to change that. By analyzing the microRNA (miRNA) in the skin of dogs with CETCL, we hope to uncover key markers that could help diagnose the disease earlier, predict how it will progress, and track treatment effectiveness. Research in humans with similar cancers has shown that identifying these miRNAs could also lead to the development of new treatment options. Ultimately, our goal is to improve the way we diagnose and care for dogs with CETCL, giving them a better chance for a longer, healthier life.
current_roster.tagline: Looking for dogs with cutaneous lymphoma
current_roster.name: Characterizing Gene Expression in Canine Cutaneous Lymphoma

current_roster.description:
Copper associated liver disease is one of the most common liver diseases in dogs and Labrador retrievers are at risk. Copper associated liver disease is caused by too much copper build up in the liver. If this disease is not diagnosed or treated, it can cause a lot of liver damage and ultimately, liver failure.


The goal of this study is to use new technologies to better understand how to diagnose these diseases with blood tests and see how they differ from Labrador retrievers with autoimmune liver disease and healthy Labrador retrievers.
current_roster.tagline: Looking for Labradors with liver disease and healthy!
current_roster.name: Copper liver disease in Labrador retrievers
current_roster.top_investigator: Tarini Ullal, Asst Professor of Clin Small Animal Int Medicine

current_roster.description:
We are conducting a research study at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital to understand how a commonly used antibiotic, cefovecin (Convenia®), affects the gut microbiome of healthy cats. While cefovecin is widely prescribed and typically well-tolerated, its long-lasting effects on the intestinal bacteria of cats have never been fully evaluated.


In this study, healthy cats ages 1–10 years will receive a single cefovecin injection, followed by a series of non-invasive fecal sample collections over 16 weeks. These samples will help us evaluate how the gut microbiota changes immediately after treatment and how long it takes to return to normal. We will also analyze whether antibiotics alter important bacterial metabolites and whether any short-term changes in gut health occur.


This research will help veterinarians better understand how antibiotics influence the feline gastrointestinal system and will contribute to improving long-term gut health and antimicrobial stewardship in cats.
current_roster.tagline: Advancing our understanding of feline gut health
current_roster.name: Seeking Healthy Cats for a Gut Microbiome Study
current_roster.top_investigator: Hannah Savage, Assistant Professor of Microbiology

current_roster.description:
Dogs with epilepsy often have normal findings on routine brain imaging, even though seizures are ongoing. This study is evaluating whether a specialized imaging technique called positron emission tomography (PET) can identify areas of abnormal brain activity in dogs with epilepsy.


By identifying functional changes in the brain, PET imaging may help veterinarians better understand seizure disorders, guide treatment decisions, and identify dogs who may benefit from new therapeutic approaches beyond standard anti-seizure medications.
current_roster.tagline: Using PET scans to better understand seizure activity in dogs
current_roster.name: Advanced Brain Imaging for Dogs with Epilepsy

current_roster.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.
current_roster.tagline: A clinical trial to characterize the clinical disease progression in dogs with glioma
current_roster.name: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description:
Feline hypersomatotropism is an endocrine disorder caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone from a pituitary tumor. This disease can lead to difficult control of diabetes, progressive organ enlargement, cardiac and renal dysfunction, and compression on of the brain by the growing tumor, ultimately causing life-threatening decompensation. To date, the surgical removal of the pituitary tumor, hypophysectomy, is the only treatment that can definitively restore normal hormone levels. 


This study explores how the immune system interacts with pituitary tumors in cats. After removal of the pituitary tumor, we will study the tumor composition and gene activity. We will also explore how immune responses relate to hormone levels, helping us better understand the link between the immune system and hormonal health. Understanding this relationship could help explain how these tumors behave and reveal promising directions for future treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Profiling the immune-endocrine interface in feline hypersomatotropism through hypophysectomy
current_roster.name: Hypophysectomy for cats with Pituitary Tumors

current_roster.description: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) or dry eye is a devastating disease that causes ocular pain and potentially blindness. It is seen more frequently in West Highland White Terriers in comparison to many other breeds. We are interested identifying the genetic components of this disease as well as characterizing this disease better through study of the microbiome and testing of the tear film and ocular surface.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find out what genes cause dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) in westies!
current_roster.name: Understanding the genes behind dry eye syndrome in West Highland white terriers

current_roster.description: Equine recurrent uveitis (ERU) is the leading cause of blindness in horses, marked by repeated episodes of inflammation of the uveal tract of the eye. Appaloosa horses, known best for their white coat spotting patterns (termed leopard complex or LP), are eight times more likely than any other breed to develop this disease and four times more likely to go blind, suggesting genetics plays a major contributing role. However, little is known about the specific genetic factors involved. The objective of this study is to determine the genetic factors contributing to ERU in multiple horse breeds.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand why horses get recurrent uveitis!
current_roster.name: Understanding the genetics causing equine recurrent uveitis in horses

current_roster.description: Oculocutaneous Syndrome is associated with the genes responsible for the white spotting in other species. We are interested in characterizing potential ocular abnormalities developing in the white-spotted Italian Greyhound dogs and identify the genetic mutations.
current_roster.name: Oculocutaneous Syndrome in Italian Greyhounds With White Spotting

current_roster.description:
Sebaceous adenitis is a skin disease caused by inflammation and eventual destruction of the sebaceous glands. The sebaceous glands are located next to the hair follicle (‘hair bed’). 
A generalized form occurs with large amounts of scale (‘dandruff’) on the skin, scale adherent to hairs and skin often dry to the touch.  As the disease progresses (often from the face or head toward the tail), there is a generalized thinning of the coat. The cause is not completely understood, but several breeds have been shown to have a higher incidence of this disease, including the Akita, thus genetics seems to play a part. Diagnosis is by clinical appearance as well as skin biopsy, which shows under the microscope either inflammation of the sebaceous glands, or a lack of sebaceous glands in the skin.

The purpose of this study is to determine if there is a difference in the DNA of Akitas with the disease sebaceous adenitis and those without the disease. There will be about 8 pets taking part in this study.  
We invite your pet to take part in this clinical trial because your dog can serve either as one of the dogs with the disease, or as a control dog if it does not have the disease. Pets that are not in a study are usually treated by certain medicated shampoos, cyclosporine, and/or retinoids. Being in this study will not affect or change any treatment the dog is currently being given.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn more about this skin disease in Akitas!
current_roster.name: Evaluating the genetic differences in Akita dogs with and without sebaceous adenitis

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to prospectively evaluate the response of nasal cancer to a combination of therapies (chemotherapy and radiation therapy) in dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find new treatments for dogs with nasal cancer!
current_roster.name: Using a combination of therapies for treatment of nasal cancer in dogs

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the outcomes for dogs treated palliatively with standard amputation (no chemotherapy). Recent data indicates that at least 35% of dogs do not appear to benefit from standard chemotherapy for this disease. To better understand whether chemotherapy is truly beneficial, this trial aims to document the outcomes prospectively and accurately for dogs whose owners have elected to treat only with surgery (amputation).

There will be about 120 dogs taking part in this study across North America. Study sites include UC Davis, Purdue University, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Tufts University and Ohio State University.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand how osteosarcoma affects dogs!
current_roster.name: Characterization of naturally occurring osteosarcoma in dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to try and improve pain control in dogs with arthritis by evaluating the blood supply to arthritic joints and pursuing a novel therapy, namely vessel embolization.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn about a new treatment for arthritis pain in dogs!
current_roster.name: Assessment of the blood supply to dog joints with arthritis and evaluation of a new technique for pain control

current_roster.description: The study compares the impact of an individually tailored MEMO plan to a standard generalized treatment plan for managing FIC symptoms and aims to identify the changes in novel blood stress biomarkers called the CTRA . Results could help improve care and outcomes for cats with chronic lower urinary tract signs.
current_roster.tagline: Reducing stress, improving health: Advancing care for cats with FIC
current_roster.name: Exploring Stress Reduction Strategies for Cats with Feline Interstitial Cystitis (FIC): A Study on Environmental Enrichment Therapy and Biomarkers

current_roster.description:
Congenital liver diseases in dogs are diseases present from birth. Examples include portal vein hypoplasia (small to absent portal veins in the liver) or ductal plate malformations (abnormal bile ducts). The purpose of this study is to describe how dogs present with these diseases and how their disease changes over their lifetime. This study is important because there are no long-term studies in dogs with these diseases so clinical course and outcomes are not known and there are no guidelines for treatment and management.


After diagnosis, blood work, urine, stool testing will be performed at 6 months, 12 months, and then yearly thereafter and will be covered as part of the study. This is an observational study so treatment is not dictated. Rather, this is a study evaluating clinical, bloodwork parameters, and overall long-term outcomes in dogs with these conditions. This is a study in collaboration with Colorado State University.
current_roster.tagline: Studying how liver diseases from birth affects health over a lifetime in dogs
current_roster.name: Portal vein hypoplasia and ductal plate malformation (blood vessel/bile duct diseases) of the liver in dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Tarini Ullal, Asst Professor of Clin Small Animal Int Medicine

current_roster.description: Canine Degenerative Myelopathy (DM) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease of dogs with no known treatments. Diagnosis of this disease is currently not possible prior to death, as it requires examination of the spinal cord under a microscope. This clinical trial is being done to test a new way to diagnose DM in dogs while they are still living, using blood and/or spinal fluid. The development of a diagnostic test before death will help us guide owner decision-making and potentially identify dogs early in their disease process for future clinical trials testing new treatments.
current_roster.tagline: Help us improve diagnosis of Degenerative Myelopathy by enrolling your dog in our study
current_roster.name: Using Spinal Fluid to Help Diagnose Degenerative Myelopathy (DM)
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, Assistant Professor

current_roster.description: This is an observational study, meaning that no treatments or medications are given as part of the research. We are simply collecting a small blood sample from dogs with pemphigus foliaceus to study how certain genes behave in the bloodstream. This information may help researchers better understand why this autoimmune skin disease develops and how it might be diagnosed or treated in the future.
current_roster.tagline: Advancing care for dogs with autoimmune skin disease
current_roster.name: Uncovering the Genetic Clues Behind Pemphigus Foliaceous

current_roster.description:
Corneal endothelial dystrophy (CED) is a devastating disease in dogs that can result in blindness and severe ocular pain from secondary complications. The endothelial cells comprise the most inner aspect of the cornea and are responsible for maintaining a proper fluid balance. This function is critical to ensuring that the cornea remains transparent for vision. In many animals, including dogs, corneal endothelial cells have a very limited capacity to regenerate following injury. In canine patients with CED, the endothelial cells degenerate until the cells still remaining can no longer function properly. This results in swelling of the cornea (edema) which results in decreased vision as well as formation of small fluid-filled blisters (bullae) on the cornea which can rupture and cause ocular discomfort. There are palliative treatments such as hypertonic saline to decrease corneal bullae formation but the only definitive treatment for this condition is a corneal transplant (penetrating keratoplasty). Unfortunately, corneal transplants are rarely performed in canine patients with CED due to the expense of the surgery and follow-up care, relatively high risk of complications, and lack of appropriate donor tissue.


Several dog breeds, including Boxers are seen more commonly for CED in comparison to other breeds. This observation suggests that this disease may have a genetic component. A similar condition called Fuch’s endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) exists in humans and several genes associated with FECD have been identified. We propose to identify the region of the dog genome associated with CED in various canine breeds. In order to do this, we will perform thorough eye examinations and use non-invasive advanced imaging techniques to examine various canine breeds including Boxers with CED and age-matched control dogs. We will collect blood from these dogs to obtain DNA. The entire canine genome will be evaluated for an association with CED. This work will be used to identify the gene(s) responsible for this condition in various canine breeds including Boxers. The ultimate goal will be to develop a genetic test for CED in Boxers.
current_roster.name: Understanding Corneal Endothelial Dystrophy in Boxers
current_roster.top_investigator: Sara M. Thomasy DVM, PhD, DACVO, Principal Investigator

current_roster.description:
For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decreased in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.
current_roster.tagline: New theragnostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer!
current_roster.name: Fluorescence Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description:
​Canine chronic enteropathy (CE) is long-term disorder of the intestinal tract in dogs, causing symptoms such as decreased appetite, vomiting, and diarrhea that significantly impact both affected dogs and their caregivers. CE is not fully understood, but may result from a complex interaction of genetics, environmental factors, changes in the gut microbiome, and an abnormal immune response.  

Current treatment strategies aim to restore intestinal balance by targeting these contributing factors. This includes altering the gut microbiota through dietary interventions, prebiotics and probiotics, and regulating  the immune system via immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive therapies. 

N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) is a naturally occurring amino sugar that has shown promise in reducing intestinal inflammation in both human and rat models of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Its mechanism of action is thought to involve enhancement of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, which plays a critical role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity and regulating immune responses. 

This study aims to investigate the potential therapeutic effects of NAG in dogs diagnosed with CE. By evaluating clinical symptoms, inflammatory markers, and microbiome composition, we aim to determine whether NAG can serve as a beneficial additional treatment for managing canine CE. ​
current_roster.tagline: A clinical trial to investigate the effects of NAG on gut health and quality of life in dogs with chronic enteropathy
current_roster.name: Investigating the effects of N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) in dogs with chronic enteropathy (CE)
